Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence at Miletus (basis of Year Established): letter of the proconsul Publius Servilius Galba to the magistrates, council and people of Miletus (Josephus, Ant. 14.244-246 = 14.10.21). A Milesian citizen, Prytanis son of Hermas, complained at Tralles that the city was attacking the Jews and forbidding them to keep the Sabbath, perform their native rites and manage their produce according to their ancestral laws; the proconsul ruled that the Jews may not be prohibited from following their customs. The source groups the letter with documents of 47-42 BCE and identifies the official with P. Servilius Isauricus, proconsul of Asia 46-44 BCE; Year of Data c. 45 BCE (Johnson/Coleman-Norton/Bourne date it 'about 45 BC', after Milesian autonomy of 46 BCE). Shows an organized resident community with its own religious practice and agricultural produce; no size given. Claims that Antiochus II (261-246 BCE) granted citizenship to the Jews of Miletus rest only on Josephus Ant. 12.125, which names 'Ionia' generally, not Miletus, so not used as documented presence.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Asia Minor': in the second half of the 1st century BCE hostility toward the Jews 'provoked at Tralles, Laodicea, Miletus, and Ephesus irritating measures' (such as seizure of Temple funds and prohibition of Jewish worship). Dated only to the second half of the 1st c. BCE; midpoint c. -25 used. Implies a resident Jewish community at Miletus; no figure. (The same article's 180,000 Jews for all of Asia Minor, derived from Flaccus' gold seizure of 62 BCE and judged perhaps ten times too high, is a regional figure, not Miletus.)

Brockhaus-Efron Jewish Encyclopedia, art. 'Milet' (vol. 11, cols. 63-64): after the Caesarian decree hostility continued; under Marcus Agrippa (c. 14 BCE) the Ionians sought to deprive the Jews of civic rights or force them to worship the Ionian gods, without success (Josephus Ant. 12.3.2). The article applies this to the Jews of Miletus; Josephus himself speaks of the Ionian cities in general, so the Miletus attribution is the encyclopedia's. Date c. 14 BCE (Agrippa in Asia). No figure. The article also mentions Alexander of Miletus (Polyhistor), a gentile author on the Jews, not evidence of Jewish residents.

BiblePlaces (Todd Bolen): 'Other evidence attests to the presence of a Jewish population in Miletus in the 1st century' (c. 1st c. CE, midpoint 50; evidence not specified). Paul's stop at Miletus (Acts 20:15-38, c. 57 CE) involves the Ephesian church elders and does not mention local Jews. Later evidence outside the period, not rowed: theatre seat inscription 'place of the Jews who are also God-fearers' (I.Milet 940; 2nd-3rd c. CE or later) and the putative synagogue at the Lion Harbour (late 4th c. CE per the Hamburg excavation, identification uncertain).
